title: How do consumer goods companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Consumer goods (FMCG) economics for case interviews: brands, retailers as customers, distribution, promotions, private label and new product launches.
hook: Consumer goods companies make money by selling branded products such as snacks, shampoo and drinks to retailers, who sell them on to shoppers, so revenue depends on how many stores stock the product, how fast it sells in each store and the net price after retailer margins and promotions. Most consumer goods cases revolve around those three numbers, plus the constant push and pull with powerful retailers who also sell their own cheaper brands.
body:
How they make money

Manufacturer revenue = stores stocking the product (distribution) × units sold per store per week (rate of sale) × net price per unit × weeks. The shopper's price is not what the manufacturer earns. Follow the price waterfall for an illustrative snack:

  • Shelf price: $2.00.
  • Retailer margin of 30% of shelf price: the manufacturer's list price is $1.40.
  • Trade spend (promotions, listing fees, display payments) of $0.20 a pack: net price is $1.20.
  • Cost to make and ship: $0.70, so gross profit is $0.50 a pack, about 42% of net price.

Marketing, sales teams and overhead come out of that $0.50. Brand building is the big discretionary cost, and the reason a strong brand can charge more than private label.

A worked example: distribution versus rate of sale

The snack is in 5,000 stores, each selling 20 packs a week at a net $1.20: 5,000 × 20 × 52 × $1.20 = $6.24M a year.

  • Getting into 1,000 more stores at the same rate adds 1,000 × 20 × 52 × $1.20 ≈ $1.25M.
  • Raising sales per store from 20 to 24 packs adds 5,000 × 4 × 52 × $1.20 ≈ $1.25M.

The two levers are worth the same, so the strategy depends on which is cheaper to achieve. Be careful, though: new stores are often weaker than existing ones. If distribution grows to 7,000 stores but average sales per store fall to 16 packs, revenue is 7,000 × 16 × 52 × $1.20 ≈ $6.99M, only 12% higher despite 40% more stores, and each extra listing may have cost a fee.

The tensions

  • Promotions lift volume, but much of the lift can be shoppers stocking up or switching from full price, and frequent deals train shoppers to buy only on promotion.
  • Private label: retailers' own brands compete on the same shelf, usually cheaper, and the retailer controls where everything goes.
  • Retailer power: a few chains often control much of the market. In Britain, Kantar's December 2025 data put the four largest grocers at about two-thirds of grocery sales (Kantar). Losing one listing can cost a brand a large share of its sales.
  • Sell-in versus sell-out: shipments to retailers (sell-in) can rise because shelves and warehouses are being filled, without shoppers buying more (sell-out). Always ask which one you are looking at.

Typical consumer goods case questions

  • Should we launch a high-protein snack? (see the product launch framework and the 4Ps)
  • Why has our market share fallen?
  • Volume grew but profit fell. Why?
  • Should we cut back on promotions?
  • Should we buy a fast-growing challenger brand?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Market share is down, so we need a bigger advertising campaign."
Strong: "I'd break the share loss into stores stocking us, availability on shelf, shoppers choosing us, how often they buy and the price they pay. If we lost a listing at one big chain, advertising won't fix it."

Common mistakes

  • Using shelf price as revenue. The manufacturer earns the net price after retailer margin and trade spend.
  • Judging promotions on volume. Judge them on extra profit, after the discount and the dip in sales afterwards.
  • Assuming new stores perform like existing ones. Model a lower rate of sale for new listings.
  • Running a marketing checklist. Let the data show which stage of the path to purchase has changed, then dig there.

Practise

1. Using the price waterfall above ($0.50 gross profit on a $1.20 net price), the manufacturer funds a $0.30-a-pack promotion. By how much must volume rise during the promotion just to keep gross profit the same?

Show the answer

Profit per pack falls from $0.50 to $0.20. Volume must be $0.50 ÷ $0.20 = 2.5 times normal, a 150% rise, before counting any dip afterwards. That is a high bar, which is why promotions should be judged on profit, not volume.

2. A brand sells 5.2M packs a year. A packaging redesign saves 5 cents a pack and costs $150k to implement. What is the payback?

Show the answer

Annual saving: 5.2M × $0.05 = $260k. Payback: $150k ÷ $260k ≈ 0.58 years, about 7 months, if volume and quality hold. A cheaper pack that stands out less on the shelf or gets damaged in transit could wipe out the saving.

3. Shipments rose 10% last quarter, but retailer sales data shows shoppers bought 2% less. What is going on, and what do you expect next quarter?

Show the answer

Retailers are building stock, perhaps for a promotion, a new listing or ahead of a price rise. Unless shopper demand recovers, shipments will fall next quarter as retailers sell through the extra stock. Base forecasts on sell-out, not sell-in.

Where to practise next

The casebook has several consumer goods cases: SnackCo (launching a protein bar), Rill Snacks (what a brand really earns through a distributor), Northstar Pet Nutrition (volume up, profit down) and Tidewell Foods (buying a challenger brand). For the retailer's side, read grocery retail cases.
